sections.h: Hosea 1-7: marriage, lawsuit and the end of the kings
sections.b: The first seven chapters hold the marriage and the three names (1-3) and the first part of the LORD's case against Israel (4-7), which runs to chapter 11: the lawsuit against the land and its priests (4) and the long indictment of Ephraim, Judah and Samaria in the years of coups and Assyrian pressure (5-7). The key words are prostitution, knowledge of God, loyal love and "turn back". This stretch ends with a nation that "turns, but not upward" (7:16).

common: Hosea spoke to the northern kingdom in the years before the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC.
uncommon: Some scholars hold that the book took its present form in Judah after 722 BC, with Judean additions.

sections.h: Gomer, the children and the sign act (1-3)
sections.b: Hosea 1 tells in the third person that the LORD told Hosea to take a wife of prostitution, that Gomer daughter of Diblaim bore a son (Jezreel), a daughter (Lo-ruhamah) and a second son (Lo-ammi), and that each name is a sentence. Chapter 2 is a speech against "the mother", ending in betrothal. Chapter 3 tells in the first person of buying back a woman who is loved by a companion and commits adultery. The commentaries differ on whether the marriage was real, whether the woman of chapter 3 is Gomer and what Gomer was when Hosea married her.

common: The marriage is a sign act that pictures the LORD's faithful love for an unfaithful people.
uncommon: The account is a vision or a parable and never happened outside the prophet's experience (Maimonides).

sections.b: In both the Hebrew and the Greek order Hosea comes first of the twelve short prophets, which the Hebrew Bible counts as one scroll. The heading in Hosea 1:1 sets the book in the eighth century BC. The Twelve move from the north's fall (Hosea, Amos) to the south's fall and its aftermath (Joel, Obadiah, Micah to Zephaniah) and to the return (Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi). Whether the Twelve were composed as one book or collected is debated.

common: The Twelve were copied together on one scroll.
uncommon: The Twelve were edited in stages with catchwords linking neighbors (Nogalski; Schart).

sections.b: In Hosea "knowledge of God" is the sum of what Israel lacks (4:1, 6) and will have (2:20; 6:3). It is joined with faithfulness and loyal love, explained as a relationship and not as information (compare Jeremiah 22:16), and set above burnt offerings (6:6). The priests are blamed first for not teaching it (4:6).
sections.refs: Hosea 2:20; Hosea 4:1; Hosea 4:6; Hosea 5:4; Hosea 6:3; Hosea 6:6

sections.b: Hosea charges that Israel credits the Baals with grain, wine, oil, wool and flax (2:5, 8, 12), keeps their festival days (2:13) and says "My Baal" where it should say "My husband" (2:16). The plural, "the Baals", shows the many local forms. Gold and silver are made "into Baal" (2:8). The LORD promises that the names of the Baals will not be remembered (2:17).

sections.h: Idols, wood and stones in Hosea 3-4
sections.b: Hosea names the practices as divination with wood and sticks (4:12), sacrifice under trees on hills (4:13), the pillar and ephod and teraphim (3:4), and, in the end, Ephraim "bound up with idols" (4:17). He treats all of it as the same offense as the Baals: asking something else for what the LORD gives.

Hosea 4:13 pictures sacrifices "on mountaintops" and "on hills", "beneath oak and poplar and terebinth, for the shade there is good", with sexual rites that involve daughters and brides, and men who "go off with prostitutes". The older view that these were organized sacred prostitution is now doubted (Bird; Budin).

Hosea mostly calls the shrine "Beth-aven", "house of wickedness" (4:15; 5:8; 10:5, 8), a play on the name Bethel, "house of God". Bethel itself is named at 10:15 and at 12:4, where Jacob met God. Hosea warns Judah not to go up to Beth-aven or enter Gilgal, nor swear "As the LORD lives" there, and at 5:8 the alarm sounds from Beth-aven toward Benjamin.
sections.refs: Hosea 4:15; Hosea 5:8; Hosea 10:5; Hosea 10:15; Hosea 12:4; Amos 4:4; 1 Kings 12:28-33

sections.b: Hosea warns Judah not to enter Gilgal (4:15), which he later says is the place of the people's evil (9:15; 12:11). Gilgal was Israel's first camp in the land and a northern shrine, named with Bethel in Amos 4:4 and 5:5.

Samaria, the capital Omri built, stands with Ephraim as the place where "evil deeds" come to light (7:1). Hosea also threatens it in 8:5-6, 10:5-7 and 13:16, where the book tells the fall plainly. In chapter 7 the court is the scene of plots against the kings.

sections.h: The blood of Jezreel and Jehu's house
sections.b: Hosea 1:4 says the LORD will bring "the blood shed at Jezreel" down on the house of Jehu, though 2 Kings 10:30 had promised Jehu four generations of sons on the throne. Scholars read the verse as a condemnation of Jehu's massacre, a charge against the later dynasty, or a word about royal murder in general. The dynasty ended with Zechariah, killed by Shallum (2 Kings 15:10).

Hosea shows Ephraim going to Assyria and sending to "King Jareb" for healing (5:13; Judah "saw his sore" but the verse does not send Judah) and Ephraim calling to Egypt and going to Assyria like a silly dove (7:11). Menahem, Hoshea and Ahaz all turned to Assyria (2 Kings 15:19-20; 16:7; 17:3), and Hosea sees these appeals as part of the same unfaithfulness as the Baal cult.

In Hosea 2:15 Israel "came up from the land of Egypt", the day of its youth, and in 7:11, 16 Ephraim calls to Egypt for help and will be mocked there. Later chapters threaten a return to Egypt (8:13; 9:3, 6; 11:5), reversing the exodus.

Hosea uses the covenant formula reversed ("you are not my people, and I will not be yours", 1:9) and restored (2:23), the lawsuit (rib, 2:2; 4:1), the betrothal gifts (2:19-20) and the covenant with the animals (2:18). In 6:7 the people "overstepped the covenant", like Adam, or at Adam.

sections.h: Marriage as the picture of the covenant
sections.b: Hosea's own marriage (1:2-3; 3:1-3), the speech against the "mother" (2:2-13) and the betrothal that ends it (2:19-20) make marriage the book's central picture of the LORD and Israel. Feminist critics ask what it does to the image of women, and defenders answer that it is aimed at Israel's leaders.
sections.refs: Hosea 1:2; Hosea 2:2; Hosea 2:19; Hosea 3:1; Jeremiah 2:2; Ezekiel 16

sections.b: Hesed is one of the three missing qualities of 4:1, the gift in the betrothal (2:19), the people's morning-cloud love (6:4) and what the LORD wants more than sacrifice (6:6). The Plain English Translation keeps "loyal love" every time, so the human and divine uses can be heard together.

The verb shuv ("turn back") is the book's word for repentance. The woman of 2:7 says "Let me go back" for her own benefit. In 3:5 the Israelites turn back and seek the LORD; in 5:4 their deeds do not let them; in 6:1 they say "Come, let us turn back" and the LORD asks what he can do with them; in 7:10 they "have not turned back".
sections.refs: Hosea 2:7; Hosea 3:5; Hosea 5:4; Hosea 6:1; Hosea 7:10; Hosea 14:1

sections.h: Hosea 6:2: "on the third day he will raise us up"
sections.b: The people of 6:1-3 hope that after two days the LORD will give them life again and on the third day raise them up. The modern consensus reads it of national restoration (compare Ezekiel 37). The Targum has "the day of the resurrection of the dead", and many Christian writers read it of Christ's resurrection "on the third day".

common: Hosea 6:2 is a hope of national recovery.
uncommon: The verse refers to the resurrection of the dead (Targum), or directly to Christ's resurrection (some Fathers).

sections.b: Paul quotes Hosea 2:23 and 1:10, in that order, for those God has called "not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles" (Romans 9:24-26), and 1 Peter 2:10 echoes the names. The Hebrew words are about the northern tribes; the churches differ on what Paul's use says about Israel and the church.
sections.refs: Hosea 1:10; Hosea 2:23; Romans 9:24; Romans 9:25; Romans 9:26; 1 Peter 2:10

sections.b: Hosea 6:6 sets loyal love and the knowledge of God above sacrifice and burnt offerings. Jesus quotes the Greek form, "Mercy is what I want, not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). Most scholars read the "not ... but" as "more than", not "instead of", and compare 1 Samuel 15:22, Micah 6:6-8 and Isaiah 1:11-17.
sections.refs: Hosea 6:6; Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7; 1 Samuel 15:22; Micah 6:6; Isaiah 1:11

sections.b: The charge of Hosea 4:4-10 is that the priests rejected knowledge and forgot the teaching of God, so the people were destroyed; the LORD rejects them as his priests, they feed on the people's sin offerings, and "like people, like priest" they will be paid back. Hosea 6:9 adds a band of priests murdering on the road to Shechem.
sections.refs: Hosea 4:6; Hosea 4:8; Hosea 4:9; Hosea 6:9; Leviticus 10:11; Malachi 2:7

sections.b: Hosea 3:4 lists ephod and teraphim among the things Israel will lack for many days. Teraphim were household images or oracle objects (Genesis 31:19; Judges 17:5; 1 Samuel 19:13), condemned in 1 Samuel 15:23 and removed by Josiah (2 Kings 23:24). Here, like the pillar, they stand beside things the law allowed, so the list describes a time with no worship at all.

The "pillar" (matstsevah) of Hosea 3:4 is a standing stone, once used for the LORD (Genesis 28:18; Exodus 24:4) and later forbidden (Deuteronomy 16:22). Hosea names it with the sacrifice, ephod and teraphim as a feature of the north's shrines that will vanish in exile.

In Hosea 2:14 the LORD leads the faithless woman out to the wilderness to "speak to her heart", and in 2:15 he turns the Valley of Achor into a door of hope, "as on the day she came up from the land of Egypt". Jeremiah 2:2 has the same picture of the wilderness as Israel's engagement.

Hosea 2:15 makes "the day she came up from the land of Egypt" the model of Israel's youth; 2:14-15 repeats the pattern of wilderness, door and land; 1:11 has the tribes go "up out of the land". Later chapters threaten a return to Egypt (8:13; 9:3) and promise a call out of it (11:1, 11).

sections.h: Hosea's marriage and the buying back of the woman
sections.b: Hosea's marriage (1:2-9) and his purchase of a woman (3:1-3) belong with the sign acts of Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel. The text does not say whether the woman was Gomer in both cases, and the Jewish tradition is divided on whether the acts were done or seen in a vision.

Hosea sees Ephraim's treaties as a form of unfaithfulness: the "lovers" of 2:5 and 8:9 are partly the nations. Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to King Jareb for healing (5:13), and "called to Egypt" and "went off to Assyria" like a silly dove (7:11).

The "many days" without king, prince, sacrifice, pillar, ephod or teraphim (3:4) and the going "up out of the land" (1:11) describe the exile of the north and a return. Many scholars think the hopes in 1:10-2:1 and 3:5 were written or expanded after the fall of Samaria.

Hosea 3:5 ends with the Israelites coming trembling to the LORD and to his goodness "in the last days" (be'acharit hayyamim), the earliest use of the phrase in the Twelve. The phrase means "in the afterward of the days" and need not mean the end of the world.
Hosea 3:5 is the book's only mention of David. Critical scholars often judge it a Judean addition; the Targum reads "Messiah the son of David", and Christian writers read it of Christ.

Wine and new wine "take away the mind" (4:11), and the princes "make themselves ill with the heat of wine" on the king's day (7:5). Hosea sets wine beside prostitution and plots as part of a court that has lost its head.

sections.h: Sin as food, as lies and as an oven
sections.b: Hosea describes sin as the priests' food (4:8), a deep slaughter (5:2), the "evil deeds" of Samaria (7:1) and an oven banked and burning (7:4-7). The same word, chatta't, means "sin" and "sin offering".

The LORD will end Israel's festival, new moon, sabbath and appointed feast (2:11), because she kept them as "the days of the Baals" (2:13). Hosea 9:5 asks what the people will do on the day of the festival when they are in exile.
The alarm sounds in Gibeah and Ramah, towns of Benjamin north of Jerusalem (5:8). Gibeah is also the place of the crime of Judges 19, to which Hosea later returns (9:9; 10:9).

sections.h: The road to Shechem in Hosea 6:9
sections.b: A band of priests "murders along the road to Shechem" (6:9). Shechem was a city of refuge and a place of covenant renewal (Joshua 20:7; 24), and the first capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:25).

The LORD says he has "hacked at them through the prophets" and killed them "with the words of my mouth" (6:5). A prophet's word does what it says. Hosea later calls the prophet a fool in the people's eyes (9:7) and says the LORD speaks through the prophets (12:10).
Judah's princes are like those who move a boundary marker (5:10), which Deuteronomy 19:14 and Proverbs 22:28 forbid as theft of family land; Isaiah 5:8 and Micah 2:2 describe the same land-grabbing.

Hosea 3:4 lists the loss of king and prince; 7:7 says "every one of their kings has fallen". Four of the last six kings of Israel were killed by their successors (2 Kings 15). Hosea sees the monarchy as part of the nation's failure (compare 8:4; 13:10).
